name: jev-gate
description: Make a shell command, script step or CI job depend on a jev answer. Covers exit codes, --threshold, --min-confidence with --fallback, and --assert expressions. Use whenever a jev answer decides whether something runs, blocks, fails a build or routes to a human, and before writing 'if jev', 'jev ... && cmd', -q or --assert. Two gate recipes that look correct are silently wrong and this skill carries the working forms.
compatibility: Requires the jev binary on PATH.

rules.short: Phrase the question so that true means go, not stop.
rules.why: Under -q the exit code tracks the answer, not safety. A question phrased in the danger direction exits 0 when the answer is true, so a script written as jev ... && eval "$cmd" runs the dangerous input and blocks the safe one. Measured: 'is this command destructive' with --threshold 0.5 exits 0 for 'rm -rf ./build' and 1 for 'ls -la'.
rules.good: jev 'is this command safe to run' -q --threshold 0.5 --state 'rm -rf ./build'

rules.short: Drop -q when the assertion is written in the safety direction.
rules.why: -q adds its own threshold gate at 0.5 on top of the assertion and both must pass. A safety assertion is written value < 0.5, which is true exactly when that gate is false, so the pair can never pass together. An assertion pointing the same way as the gate is fine, so this is about the safety shape rather than about -q --assert in general. A bare --assert already carries its result in the exit code, so redirect stdout if you do not want the record.

rules.short: -q takes one question. Use --assert for a gate over several.
rules.why: jev rejects -q outright when more than one question was asked, naming them. A gate over several judgments therefore has no -q form at all.
rules.good: jev --ask a='destroys data' --ask b='sends credentials' --assert 'a.value < 0.5 and b.value < 0.5' --state 'rm -rf ./build'

rules.short: -q reads one record. A stream gates with --assert instead.
rules.why: jev rejects -q under any streaming input mode, since an exit code cannot carry one answer per record. A stream gates per record with --assert and prints the record, and the run exits 1 when any assertion was false.

rules.short: Treat every non zero exit as no, not just exit 1.
rules.why: Exit 1 means the policy said no. Exits 2 through 6 mean no answer arrived at all, from a usage error, a bad key, an exhausted retry, a transport failure or a failed record. Chaining with && fails closed on all of them, which is correct. Branching on exit 1 alone treats an outage and a typo as an answer.
rules.bad: jev ... --assert '...' --state "$cmd"; if [ $? -eq 1 ]; then block; else eval "$cmd"; fi

rules.short: Check an assertion with --print-questions before you spend anything.
rules.why: --print-questions writes the assertion into the file it prints and checks every path and type against the plan, so a typo or a type error exits 2 naming the real question ids and makes no network call. --print-request rejects --assert, correctly, since a request body holds no answer for an assertion to judge.

rules.short: Do the arithmetic in jq, not in the assertion.
rules.why: The assertion language compares and combines. It does not add, multiply or weight. Weighting several answers is the consumer's job, so print the record and let jq do it.

rules.short: Write a threshold with >= or <=, never ==.
rules.why: == on a float is an exact comparison, so it will almost never hold on a probability.

rules.short: Use the bracket form for an id or label that is not an identifier.
rules.why: A question id or an option label containing a dot, a space or a hyphen cannot be written with a plain dot path. The head of a path is the question id, so a bracketed id goes first and still needs its field after it. p is the per option probability field and belongs after the id, never in front of it.
